                                        II.   MOTION FOR CLASS CERTIFICATION
                                  14
                                              A.    Legal Standard for Class Certification
                                  15
                                              Before it can certify a class, a district court must be “satisfied, after a rigorous analysis,
                                  16
                                       that the prerequisites” of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23 have been satisfied. Olean Wholesale
                                  17
                                       Grocery Coop., Inc. v. Bumble Bee Foods LLC, 31 F.4th 651, 664–65 (9th Cir. 2022) (quoting
                                  18
                                       Gen. Tel. Co. of Sw. v. Falcon, 457 U.S. 147, 161 (1982)). “Frequently that ‘rigorous analysis’
                                  19
                                       will entail some overlap with the merits of the plaintiff’s underlying claim. That cannot be
                                  20
                                       helped.” Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338, 351 (2011).
                                  21
                                              Rule 23 consists of two parts. Fed. R. Civ. P. 23. First, Plaintiff must satisfy all four
                                  22
                                       requirements of Rule 23(a): “One or more members of a class may sue or be sued as representative
                                  23
                                       parties on behalf of all members only if: (1) the class is so numerous that joinder of all members is
                                  24
                                       impracticable; (2) there are questions of law or fact common to the class; (3) the claims or
                                  25
                                       defenses of the representative parties are typical of the claims or defenses of the class; and (4) the
                                  26
                                       representative parties will fairly and adequately protect the interests of the class.” Olean, 31 F.4th
                                  27
                                       at 663; Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(a). Second, Plaintiff must demonstrate through evidentiary proof that
                                  28
                                                                                          4
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT              Document 314          Filed 06/16/26    Page 5 of 13




                                   1   the class satisfies at least one of the three subsections under Rule 23(b). Comcast Corp. v.

                                   2   Behrend, 569 U.S. 27, 33 (2013). Classes certified under Rule 23(b)(3) require that “questions of

                                   3   law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual

                                   4   members, and that a class action is superior to other available methods for fairly and efficiently

                                   5   adjudicating the controversy.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3).

                                   6               “Rule 23 grants courts no license to engage in free-ranging merits inquiries at the

                                   7   certification stage. Merits questions may be considered to the extent—but only to the extent—that

                                   8   they are relevant to determining whether the Rule 23 prerequisites for class certification are

                                   9   satisfied.” Amgen Inc. v. Conn. Ret. Plans & Tr. Funds, 568 U.S. 455, 466 (2013). For example,

                                  10   to determine whether a common question prerequisite is satisfied, “a district court is limited to

                                  11   resolving whether the evidence establishes that a common question is capable of classwide

                                  12   resolution, not whether the evidence in fact establishes that plaintiffs would win at trial.” Olean,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   31 F.4th at 666–67.

                                  14   III.        DISCUSSION
                                  15               Defendant argues that (1) Plaintiff does not identify a common question of fact and (2)

                                  16   individual questions predominate the class. ECF 215-1 at 17. Plaintiff argues that the question of

                                  17   what information was shared without consent satisfies the commonality requirement of Rule 23(a)

                                  18   and argues that individualized questions of proof do not predominate either the statewide or

                                  19   nationwide classes. ECF 259-1 at 8–20.

                                  20          A.      Plaintiff’s Classes Present No Choice of Law Issue

                                  21               After Defendant made an objection to the application of California law to the nationwide

                                  22   class “Plaintiffs limit[ed] their nationwide classes to the federal ECPA claim” and Plaintiff further

                                  23   state that they “will pursue negligence and unjust enrichment only on behalf of the California

                                  24   subclasses” ECF 258 at 9. Plaintiff later clarified that Plaintiff limits its California statutory claims

                                  25   (CIPA and CCPA) to the California subclasses. ECF 287. Plaintiff’s limitations defeat any choice

                                  26   of law issues which might have otherwise arisen with the nationwide class.

                                  27               Accordingly, Plaintiff must make specific showings to certify the proposed nationwide

                                  28   class certification pursuant to the ECPA. The ECPA “prohibits unauthorized ‘interception’ of an
                                                                                             5
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT           Document 314          Filed 06/16/26     Page 6 of 13




                                   1   ‘electronic communication.’” Meta Platforms, 690 F. Supp. 3d at 1075 (citing In re Facebook,

                                   2   Inc. Internet Tracking Litig., 956 F.3d at 606–07). The one-party consent exemption provides that

                                   3   it is not unlawful for “a person not acting under color of law to intercept a wire, oral, or electronic

                                   4   communication” when that person is a party to the communication “or where one of the parties to

                                   5   the communication has given prior consent to such interception unless such communication is

                                   6   intercepted” to commit a crime or tort. 18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d).

                                   7          Plaintiff’s California subclasses require separate showings based on California law. “To

                                   8   state a claim for negligence in California, a plaintiff must establish the following elements: (1) the

                                   9   defendant had a duty, or an ‘obligation to conform to a certain standard of conduct for the

                                  10   protection of others against unreasonable risks,’ (2) the defendant breached that duty, (3) that

                                  11   breach proximately caused the plaintiff’s injuries, and (4) damages.” Bass v. Facebook, Inc., 394

                                  12   F. Supp. 3d 1024, 1038–39 (N.D. Cal. 2019) (internal citations omitted).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          The CCPA provides a limited civil cause of action for any “consumer whose nonencrypted

                                  14   and nonredacted personal information… is subject to an unauthorized access and exfiltration,

                                  15   theft, or disclosure as a result of the business’s violation of the duty to implement and maintain

                                  16   reasonable security practices.” Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.150(a)(1). Under the CCPA, “[a] third

                                  17   party shall not sell or share personal information about a consumer that has been sold to, or shared

                                  18   with, the third party by a business unless the consumer has received explicit notice and is provided

                                  19   an opportunity to exercise the right to opt-out.” Id. § 1798.115.

                                  20          “To allege unjust enrichment as an independent cause of action, a plaintiff must show that

                                  21   the defendant received an unjustly retained a benefit at the plaintiff’s expense.” Katz-Lacabe v.

                                  22   Oracle Am., Inc., 668 F. Supp. 3d 928, 945 (N.D. Cal. 2023).

                                  23          Finally, California Penal Code § 631(a)(2) applies to anyone who:

                                  24
                                                      (2) willfully and without the consent of all parties to the
                                  25                  communication, or in any unauthorized manner, reads, or attempts to
                                                      read, or to learn the contents or meaning of any message ... while the
                                  26                  same is in transit or passing over any wire, line, or cable, or is being
                                                      sent from, or received at any place within this state
                                  27

                                  28
                                                                                          6
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT           Document 314          Filed 06/16/26      Page 7 of 13




                                   1   Section 637.2 provides a civil cause of action for damages or an injunction to anyone “injured by a

                                   2   violation of this chapter . . . against the person who committed the violation . . . [.]” Cal. Pen.

                                   3   Code § 637.2. Section 632 punishes a person who “intentionally and without the consent of all

                                   4   parties to a confidential communication, uses an electronic amplifying or recording device to

                                   5   eavesdrop upon or record the confidential communication.” Cal. Pen. Code § 632(a).

                                   6          Because Plaintiff limits the federal claims to the nationwide class and the state law claims

                                   7   to the California class, no choice of law issue is present.

                                   8          B.    Numerosity
                                   9          Rule 23(a)(1) requires that “the class is so numerous that joinder of all members is

                                  10   impracticable.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(a)(1). The party seeking certification “do[es] not need to state

                                  11   the exact number of potential class members, nor is a specific number of members required for

                                  12   numerosity.” In re Rubber Chems. Antitrust Litig., 232 F.R.D. 346, 350 (N.D. Cal. 2005). Courts
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   in this district generally agree that numerosity is satisfied if the class includes “40 or more

                                  14   members.” Furthermore, numerosity is satisfied “where the exact size of the proposed class is

                                  15   unknown, but general knowledge and common sense indicate it is large.” Pardi v. Tricida, Inc.,

                                  16   No. 21-cv-00076, 2024 WL 4336627, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 27, 2024)

                                  17          The Court may properly conclude that numerosity is satisfied because, based on the

                                  18   number of credit card applications Capital One received during the Class Period, the number of

                                  19   plaintiffs is likely to exceed the threshold amount courts generally find satisfy numerosity. See

                                  20   ECF 187-1 at 20 (Plaintiffs allege that August 2021 to August 2024 Capital One received millions

                                  21   of credit applications); Villalpando v. Exel Direct Inc., 303 F.R.D. at 605–06 (finding numerosity

                                  22   satisfied with 40 or more plaintiffs); see also In re Facebook, Inc., PPC Adver. Litig., 282 F.R.D.

                                  23   446, 452 (N.D. Cal. 2012) (“[C]ourts generally find that the numerosity factor is satisfied if the

                                  24   class comprises 40 or more members”).

                                  25          Accordingly, the court finds that Plaintiff satisfies the numerosity requirement of Rule

                                  26   23(a)(1).

                                  27          C.    Commonality & Predominance
                                  28          Courts have found it appropriate to assess Rule 23(a)(2) commonality and Rule 23(b)(3)
                                                                                          7
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT           Document 314          Filed 06/16/26     Page 8 of 13




                                   1   predominance together. In re Capacitors Antitrust Litig. (No. III), No. 14-CV-03264, 2018 WL

                                   2   5980139, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 14, 2018) (citing See, e.g., Just Film, Inc. v. Buono, 847 F.3d

                                   3   1108, 1120-21 (9th Cir. 2017)); see also Frasco v. Flo Health, Inc., 349 F.R.D. 557, 574 (N.D.

                                   4   Cal. 2025); White v. Symetra Assigned Benefits Serv. Co., 104 F.4th 1182, 1191 (9th Cir. 2024)

                                   5   (citing Olean Wholesale Grocery Coop., Inc. v. Bumble Bee Foods LLC, 31 F.4th 651, 664 (9th

                                   6   Cir. 2022) (en banc) (“The commonality and predominance inquiries overlap.”). Thus, after

                                   7   separating questions common to the legal claims of the class from those that “present

                                   8   individualized issues,” courts “analyze whether the common questions predominate over the

                                   9   individual questions.” DZ Rsrv. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 96 F.4th 1223, 1233 (9th Cir. 2024). In

                                  10   essence, this inquiry “asks whether the common, aggregation-enabling, issues in the case are more

                                  11   prevalent or important than the non-common, aggregation-defeating, individual issues.” Tyson

                                  12   Foods, Inc. v. Bouaphakeo, 577 U.S. 442, 453 (2016).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Rule 23(a)(2) requires that “there are questions of law or fact common to the class.” Fed.

                                  14   R. Civ. P. (a)(2). “A common contention need not be one that ‘will be answered, on the merits, in

                                  15   favor of the class.’ It only ‘must be of such nature that it is capable of class-wide resolution.’”

                                  16   Alcantar v. Hobart Servs., 800 F.3d 1047, 1053 (9th Cir. 2015) (quoting Amgen, 568 U.S. at 459

                                  17   and Dukes, 564 U.S. at 350). At the center of this inquiry is “the capacity of a classwide

                                  18   proceeding to generate common answers apt to drive the resolution of the litigation.” Dukes, 564

                                  19   U.S. at 350. “[A]s in all class actions, commonality cannot be determined without a precise

                                  20   understanding of the nature of the underlying claims.” Parsons v. Ryan, 754 F.3d 657, 676 (9th

                                  21   Cir. 2014). Plaintiffs need not show, however, that “every question in the case, or even a

                                  22   preponderance of questions, is capable of class wide resolution. So long as there is ‘even a single

                                  23   common question,’ a would-be class can satisfy the commonality requirement of Rule 23(a)(2).”

                                  24   Wang v. Chinese Daily News, Inc., 737 F.3d 538, 544 (9th Cir.2013) (quoting Dukes, 564 U.S. at

                                  25   359, 131 S.Ct. 2541)

                                  26          The predominance inquiry of Rule 23(b)(3) “tests whether proposed classes are sufficiently

                                  27   cohesive to warrant adjudication by representation.” Amchem Prods., Inc. v. Windsor, 521 U.S.

                                  28   591, 623 (1997). Accordingly, the predominance analysis “focuses on the relationship between the
                                                                                          8
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT           Document 314         Filed 06/16/26     Page 9 of 13




                                   1   common and individual issues in the case.” Wang v. Chinese Daily News, Inc., 737 F.3d 538, 545

                                   2   (9th Cir.2013) (internal quotation marks omitted); see also In re Wells Fargo Home Mortgage

                                   3   Overtime Pay Litig., 571 F.3d 953, 958 (9th Cir.2009) (“Whether judicial economy will be served

                                   4   in a particular case turns on close scrutiny of the relationship between the common and individual

                                   5   issues.” (internal quotation marks omitted)). “[I]f the discovery and trial process must assess

                                   6   thousands of claims one claim at a time, then the individualized issue will weigh heavy in the

                                   7   predominance balancing.” In re Meta Pixel Tax Filing Cases Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 22-CV-

                                   8   07557, 2026 WL 1025741, at *10 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 30, 2026) (citation omitted).

                                                        Common Question, but Requires Individualized Proof

                                              Capital One argues that class certification is not appropriate because there is no uniform set
                                  11

                                  12

                                       specific information transmitted via a specific technology may vary from class member to class
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       member. ECF 215-1 at 16. Plaintiff argues that Capital One uniformly deployed a broad
                                  14

                                       common questions.” Griffith v. TikTok, Inc., 2024 WL 4308813, at *10 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 9, 2024)

                                   1   influence what information is shared and when. Moreover, not every application Plaintiff

 United States District Court

                                  16               ii.   Consent Requires Individualized Proof
                                  17            Plaintiff argues that the consent inquiry does present a predominance issue because the

                                  18   disclosures occurred according to a uniform privacy policy and because the disclosures’

                                  19   inadequacies apply to all class members. ECF 259-1 at 10–13. Defendant argues that consent

                                  20   presents individualized questions that defeat predominance because class members were exposed

                                  21   to a mix of disclosures and developed different understandings of those disclosures. ECF 215-1 at

                                  22   20–22.

                                  23            Courts recognize that the consent inquiry focuses on “a user’s subjective understanding of

                                  24   the terms of the relevant agreement” and accounts for “a broad set of materials.” Calhoun v.

                                  25   Google LLC, 349 F.R.D. 588, 597 n.3 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (emphasis added) (denying certification on

                                  26   consent grounds); see also In re Google Inc. Gmail Litigation, 2014 WL 1102660, at *16 (N.D.

                                  27   Cal. Mar. 18, 2014) (denying class certification for class which included CIPA and ECPA claims

                                  28   because consent is an “intensely factual question” requiring “consideration of the circumstances”
                                                                                        10
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT         Document 314            Filed 06/16/26   Page 11 of 13




                                   1   “to divine whether the party whose [data] was intercepted was on notice that the [data] would be

                                   2   intercepted.”).

                                   3          Here, in order to submit an application with Capital One, each putative class member

                                   4   agreed to Capital One’s privacy policy. ECF 215-1 at 20. Moreover, depending on whether the

                                   5   applicant resides in California, that applicant will receive additional disclosures. ECF 214 at 73.

                                   6   Whether inquiring into class members express or implied consent, individualized questions of fact

                                   7   will predominate over common questions. For express consent, the Court would need to grapple

                                   8   with the “diversity of disclosures” that putative class members were exposed to. In re Google Inc.

                                   9   Gmail Litigation, 2014 WL 1102660, at *15. Any inquiry into implied consent would require the

                                  10   Court to “evaluate to which of the various sources each individual user had been exposed and

                                  11   whether each individual knew about and consented to the interception based on the sources to

                                  12   which she was exposed.” Id. (citation omitted).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Accordingly, the Court finds that the issue of consent requires individualized inquiries that

                                  14   will overwhelm any common questions.

                                  15              iii.   Standing Requires Individualized Proof
                                  16          The Supreme Court has not yet decided whether a class may be certified under Rule

                                  17   23(b)(3) when the class includes both injured and uninjured class members. See Lab’y Corp. of

                                  18   Am. Holdings v. Davis, 145 S. Ct. 1608 (2025) (dismissing writ of certiorari on this issue as

                                  19   improvidently granted). In the Ninth Circuit, a class may be certified where the plaintiff has

                                  20   demonstrated a method of proof that is capable of showing harm on a class-wide basis, even if the

                                  21   class potentially includes more than a de minimis number of uninjured class members. See Olean

                                  22   Wholesale Grocery Coop., Inc. v. Bumble Bee Foods LLC, 31 F.4th 651, 669, 681 (9th Cir. 2022).

                                  23          Plaintiff argues that TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) requires that

                                  24   unnamed class members show standing only after certification. ECF 259-1 at 13. However,

                                  25   “although TransUnion calls into question whether courts at the class certification stage should

                                  26   assess the standing of putative class members, it ultimately provides no basis for this Court to

                                  27   disregard binding Ninth Circuit law on point.” Stiner v. Brookdale Senior Living, Inc., 665 F.

                                  28   Supp. 3d 1150, 1182 (N.D. Cal. 2023), opinion clarified, No. 17-cv-03962, 2024 WL 3498492
                                                                                         11
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT          Document 314           Filed 06/16/26    Page 12 of 13




                                   1   (N.D. Cal. July 22, 2024) (citing Lauderdale v. NFP Ret., Inc., No. SA-cv-2:13-01, 2022 WL

                                   2   1599916, at *4 (C.D. Cal. Feb. 16, 2022)) (“Nothing in TransUnion indicates that it changed

                                   3   settled Ninth Circuit law regarding what it is required to demonstrate standing at the class

                                   4   certification stage.”). Thus, the Court must determine whether Plaintiff has presented a method of

                                   5   proof capable of showing harm on a class-wide basis. King v. Nat’l Gen. Ins. Co., No. 15-cv-

                                   6   00313, 2025 WL 2021884, at *2 (N.D. Cal. July 18, 2025).

                                   7          The Court finds that Plaintiff has not. The Court’s written Order on May 22, 2026 is

                                   8   illustrative on this point. There, the Court found that one named plaintiff could demonstrate

                                   9   Article III standing in alleging that personal and financial data which Plaintiff Williams had

                                  10   demonstrated an actual expectation of privacy in was transmitted using Defendant’s tracking

                                  11   technology, while another, Plaintiff Ingram, had not demonstrated an expectation of privacy in

                                  12   their date. ECF 304. The Court would need to engage in this same, fact-intensive inquiry for each
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   prospective plaintiff. That is, the Court would need to determine what, if any, data was shared,

                                  14   how that data was shared, for what purpose the data was shared, and the nature of that data shared

                                  15   with respect to each plaintiff. Plaintiff has not demonstrated a method for answering those

                                  16   questions on a classwide basis sufficient to satisfy Rule 23’s predominance requirement. See

                                  17   Ambrosio v. Progressive Preferred Ins. Co., 154 F.4th 1107, 1112 (9th Cir. 2025) (holding that

                                  18   Circuit has also held that common issues do not predominate where “figuring out whether each

                                  19   individual putative class member was harmed would involve an inquiry specific to that person.”).

                                  20          As noted in the Court’s May 22, 2026 Order, the standing analysis applies to Plaintiff’s

                                  21   statutory and common law claims. ECF 304 at 6 (citing Krzyzek v. OpenX Techs., Inc., No. 25-cv-

                                  22   05588, 2026 WL 206855, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 27, 2026) (analyzing Article III standing as a

                                  23   threshold issue on all claims where plaintiffs brought a putative class action for common law

                                  24   privacy claims, unjust enrichment, violations of CIPA, and ECPA)). Thus, the Court’s finding that

                                  25   class certification is inappropriate in this action due to individualized inquiries of standing applies

                                  26   to both Plaintiff’s California and nationwide classes.

                                  27          Accordingly, the Court finds that issues of Article III standing provide an additional

                                  28   ground for denying class certification here.

                                   2            For the reasons discussed above, the Court finds that Plaintiff has not met the

                                   3   predominance requirement of Rule 23(b)(3) to certify a nationwide or statewide class.

                                   4   IV.      CONCLUSION
                                   5            For the reasons stated above, the Plaintiff’s motion for class certification is DENIED. The
